summary: This informational memo describes Microsoft Point-to-Point Compression, a way to compress packets carried over PPP links. It documents a vendor method rather than an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Squeezing your clothes into a vacuum bag so more fits in the same suitcase.

subtitle: Compression scheme for Point-to-Point Protocol data on dial-up links

tldr.problem: Dial-up internet connections had limited bandwidth, and compressing the data sent over PPP links could improve throughput and user experience.
tldr.mechanism: MPPC uses an LZ-based sliding window compression algorithm with an 8192-byte history buffer, encoding literals and copy tuples to represent data more compactly. A coherency count keeps compressor and decompressor synchronized.
tldr.outcome: MPPC was a vendor-specific solution from Microsoft, implemented in products using PPP but not adopted as an Internet standard. The compression can be negotiated and disabled if it causes data expansion.

today: RFC 2118 is an informational document describing Microsoft's MPPC, a vendor-specific compression protocol for PPP links. It was used in Windows dial-up implementations but was not standardized by the IETF. Modern broadband connections have made compression on PPP links largely obsolete.

sections.title: Compression for PPP Links
sections.content:
The Microsoft Point-to-Point Compression protocol (MPPC) is a method for reducing the size of data sent over PPP links. MPPC is an LZ-based algorithm (named after Lempel and Ziv), which maintains a sliding window history buffer of the data already sent. The algorithm is optimized for the typical PPP scenario with 1500-byte Maximum Transmission Units (MTU).

The RFC notes that MPPC requires licensing: it can only be used in products that implement PPP and is licensed by Stac Electronics on a non-discriminatory basis. This document is informational and describes a vendor method rather than an Internet standard.

MPPC keeps 8192 bytes of history, so after 8192 bytes of data have been transmitted, there is always 8192 bytes of history available for future compression, except when the history is intentionally flushed.
sections.plainLanguage: MPPC is a way to make data smaller before sending it over internet connections, keeping a memory of what was sent before to find patterns.

sections.title: Negotiating MPPC
sections.content:
Before any MPPC packets are sent, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP) must reach the Opened state. The CCP Configuration Option for MPPC has type 18 and length 6 octets, with a 4-octet Supported Bits field where the least significant bit indicates desire to negotiate MPPC. All other bits must be zero.

MPPC packets are marked with PPP Protocol type hex 00FD when compression is successfully negotiated. The maximum length of a compressed MPPC datagram is limited by the 8192-byte history buffer, so the datagram cannot exceed 8192 bytes. Padding is not recommended with MPPC since it defeats the purpose of compression; if padding is necessary, self-describing padding should be negotiated during the LCP phase.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using MPPC, the two sides talk using CCP to agree to use compression. MPPC-compressed packets are marked with a special number so both sides know they are compressed.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Header Bits
sections.content:
An MPPC packet begins with the PPP Protocol field (2 octets), followed by a 2-octet flags and coherency count field, then the compressed data. The protocol field indicates what type of data is compressed (normally the range hex 0021 to hex 00FA). Only packets in this range are passed through MPPC; others are sent uncompressed with their original protocol numbers.

Four control bits follow the protocol field: Bit A (FLUSHED) indicates the history buffer was just initialized, so the packet can always be decompressed. Bit B indicates the packet data was moved to the front of the history buffer due to buffer space constraints. Bit C indicates the packet is compressed. Bit D must be zero.

The Coherency Count is a 12-bit value that ensures packets are received in order and none are dropped. It starts at zero and increments by 1 for each packet, wrapping around when all bits are 1. If the receiver's coherency count does not match the packet's count, synchronization is lost and must be restored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has special bits that tell the receiver if the compression was reset, if data was moved around in memory, or if the packet is even compressed at all.

sections.title: Compression Encoding Scheme
sections.content:
MPPC produces either Literals (uncompressed bytes) or Copy tuples (offset and length pairs) as it processes data. The compressor scans the data frame looking for matches in the history buffer. When a match is found, it encodes the offset (how many bytes back in history) and length-of-match (how many bytes to copy).

Literals below hex 80 are encoded as themselves. Literals with values hex 80 and above are encoded as bits 10 followed by their lower 7 bits. Offset encoding uses different bit patterns depending on the offset value: offsets below 64 use bits 1111, offsets 64-320 use bits 1110, and offsets 320-8191 use bits 110.

Length encoding follows a similar pattern with multiple ranges. A length of 3 is encoded as a single 0 bit. Lengths 4-7 use bits 10, lengths 8-15 use bits 110, and progressively longer prefixes are used for larger lengths, up to length 8191 encoded as bits 111111111110 followed by 12 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The compression scheme has special codes for short repeated bytes and for finding matching patterns in history, making common data much smaller.

sections.title: Synchronization and Reliability
sections.content:
MPPC does not require a reliable link but uses the coherency count to keep history buffers synchronized. If the receiver's expected coherency count does not match the received count, the receiver drops the packet and sends a CCP Reset-Request. When the compressor receives this request, it flushes its history buffer and sets the FLUSHED bit in the next outgoing packet.

When the decompressor receives a packet with the FLUSHED bit set, it flushes its history buffer and sets its coherency count to match the compressor's transmitted count. This achieves synchronization without needing a CCP Reset-Ack packet, allowing recovery from packet loss.

If compression would result in data expansion (the compressed form is larger than the original), MPPC sends the original data uncompressed as an MPPC packet, flushes the history, and sets the FLUSHED bit on the next compressed packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The coherency count is like a sequence number that helps both sides stay in sync if packets are lost or arrive out of order.
